comments.text: Life-Giving but Lethal: The Culprit Behind Dead Zones and the Threat to Our Water Supply == The unchecked flow of phosphorus into our waterways — often from farm runoff — contributes to “dead zones” and toxic algae blooms. At the same time, as an essential ingredient in fertilizer, phosphorus turns vast swaths of land green, nourishing crops and animals. It makes life possible for billions of people.

I remember as a kid in the early eighties, people would say things like "when the air is too dirty to breath, when it's not safe to go outside, that's when we'll start acting to reduce pollution. By the end of the decade summer air quality was regularly bad enough to be a health risk in the summer, and we still didn't do anything. Smog days became a normal part of summer. In 2003 we finally committed to phasing out coal plants in , and got rid of the last one in 2014. The results were fast: we had 53 smog days in 2005 at the beginning of the phase out, and 0 in 2014 when it was completed. In the context of the current heat and air quality crises (and the that causes them), this highlights how good we are at accommodating objectively horrifying conditions. And, should we decide to act, how much we can accomplish if we decide we don't want to live with the horror anymore.
